title: Garden Tools
cardDescription: Hand tools and everyday helpers for tending a garden.
description: Picture the familiar jobs of digging, watering, and supporting plants as you work through this easy garden-tool crossword.
focus: This puzzle stays in the tool shed: digging, carrying, watering, and keeping plants supported. The answers name tools and supplies rather than flowers or vegetables, so each clue gives you a specific garden job to picture.
solvingTip: Look for the job in the clue. A tool for lifting soil is different from one for gathering leaves. At a crossing, check both words before changing a letter that already fits.

Long-handled tool with teeth for gathering leaves
Flexible tube that carries water to a garden
Digging tool with a flat, rectangular blade

Protective coverings worn on the hands
Small wheeled vehicle for carrying garden supplies
Round container with a handle for carrying water

Protective garment tied over clothes while working
A watering ___ has a handle and a spout

A pointed post used to support a growing plant
The part of a garden tool held in the hand
Device that applies liquid as a fine mist
Round part that lets a garden cart roll
Bristled tool for cleaning dirt from garden equipment

answerNotes.TROWEL: A trowel is sized for one hand and small planting holes. A shovel is larger and suited to moving more soil, which is why the clues distinguish a hand tool from a broad scoop.
answerNotes.SPADE: A spade is typically associated with a flat blade and straight cutting edge. A shovel generally has a more scooped blade, although everyday names for the two can overlap.
answerNotes.TWINE: Twine is a strong string. Gardeners use it to fasten stems to supports, leaving room for the plant to grow instead of tying a tight knot around the stem.
answerNotes.FORK: A garden fork has sturdy tines for working soil. The garden context separates it from the smaller fork used at a dinner table.
answerNotes.STAKE: A stake is a support post, not the string used to fasten a plant to it. The clue asks for the post itself.
answerNotes.CAN: A watering can is a portable container with a spout. The fill-in-the-blank clue supplies 'watering' so the short answer is the container's name.

title: Spring Flowers
cardDescription: Recognizable spring flowers and the parts of a bloom.
description: Take a stroll past tulips, daffodils, and other familiar blooms in this gentle spring-flower crossword.
focus: The clues focus on recognizable garden flowers and the visible parts of a bloom. They use common names rather than Latin plant names. Flowering dates vary with climate, so seasonal clues refer to familiar patterns rather than a fixed month.
solvingTip: Start with a flower name you recognize. Short answers about flower parts can help you cross into a longer name. If two flowers seem possible, use the number of squares and the crossing letters together.
words: Spring flower with a cup-shaped bloom, often grown from a bulb
Spring flower with a trumpet-shaped center, often yellow
Flower with bearded varieties and a name shared with part of the eye
Small, cup-shaped flower often among the first to bloom after winter
Shrub known for fragrant clusters of purple or white flowers
Garden flower whose markings can look like a little face
Garden flower known for large, many-petaled blooms in late spring
Flowering shrub related to the rhododendron
One of the colored parts surrounding a flower's center

Underground storage structure from which a tulip grows
Small flower whose name is also a shade of purple
Early-blooming flower whose name ends in 'rose'
The color made by mixing red and blue, seen in many irises
A pale red color seen in many spring flowers
The color of snow and many daffodil petals

answerNotes.DAFFODIL: The central trumpet is a useful visual clue for a daffodil. Its surrounding petal-like parts make the bloom easy to recognize even when the color is not yellow.
answerNotes.BULB: A bulb stores resources underground. Tulips and daffodils grow from bulbs; a bulb is not the same thing as a seed.
answerNotes.CROCUS: Crocuses are often associated with the first flowers after winter. They grow from corms, which are underground storage structures distinct from true bulbs.
answerNotes.BUD: A bud is an unopened stage of a flower. Bloom can describe an open flower, making these two short answers useful contrasts.
answerNotes.LILAC: Lilac commonly names both a flowering shrub and a pale purple color. In this puzzle, the clue describes the fragrant shrub.
answerNotes.PETAL: Petals are the colored parts around the center of many flowers. The clue asks for one part, so the answer is singular.

title: The Vegetable Patch
cardDescription: Everyday crops you might grow in a kitchen garden.
description: Explore familiar kitchen-garden crops, from crisp roots to leafy greens, with clear clues about what each plant produces.
focus: This puzzle follows the edible harvest: roots, leaves, pods, and familiar salad ingredients. The clues distinguish the part we eat and use everyday American food names. There are no growing-zone numbers or specialist gardening abbreviations to decode.
solvingTip: Notice whether the clue describes a root, leaf, or pod. That small detail can separate several vegetables with similar lengths. A clue for one vegetable takes a singular answer unless it explicitly asks for more than one.
words: Orange root vegetable often eaten raw or cooked
Red salad fruit that grows on a vine
Small round green vegetable found in a pod
Leafy vegetable often used as the base of a green salad
Small, peppery root vegetable often red outside and white inside
Layered vegetable that can make your eyes water when cut
Leafy green often sold with curly leaves
Vegetable with kernels growing on a cob

Leafy head vegetable often shredded for coleslaw
Vegetable with crisp stalks often served with peanut butter

Bell ___: a hollow vegetable sold in green, red, and other colors

Long green salad vegetable often used to make pickles
Round root vegetable often white below and purple near the top

answerNotes.TOMATO: A tomato is botanically a fruit because it develops from a flower and contains seeds. It still belongs in a kitchen-garden puzzle, where it is commonly treated as a vegetable in cooking.
answerNotes.POTATO: A potato is a tuber, an enlarged underground stem. Carrots and radishes are roots; the different plant parts give the clues more precise meanings.
answerNotes.PEA: The word 'small' describes the vegetable, not the length of a plural answer. This clue asks for one pea, which fits three squares.
answerNotes.CABBAGE: Coleslaw is a useful everyday association for cabbage. Lettuce also forms leafy heads, so the serving example helps separate the two.
answerNotes.SQUASH: Squash names a group that includes summer types such as zucchini and winter types such as butternut. The clue intentionally names both.
answerNotes.BEET: Beets are often red, but some varieties are golden. The clue allows both while still pointing to the familiar root vegetable.

title: Backyard Wildlife
cardDescription: Birds, pollinators, and other small backyard visitors.
description: Meet the birds, insects, and other small animals you might notice while spending a quiet moment in the yard.
focus: This puzzle looks beyond the plants to the living things around them. Some clues describe an animal's body or movement; others name something it builds. The collection includes pollinators, birds, and occasional nibblers rather than treating every visitor as a pest.
solvingTip: Look for the distinguishing detail: honey, a shell, a web, or a long pair of ears. A clue about something an animal builds asks for the object, not the animal that made it.
words: Common American songbird with an orange-red breast
Honey-making insect that carries pollen between flowers
Insect that begins as a caterpillar and later has broad, colorful wings
Long, legless animal often found wriggling in garden soil

answerNotes.LADYBUG: Ladybug is the familiar American name for this beetle; ladybird is common in British English. Many ladybugs feed on aphids, making them welcome garden visitors.
answerNotes.SPIDER: Spiders have eight legs and are arachnids, not insects. Insects such as ants and bees have six legs, a distinction that makes this clue specific.
answerNotes.NEST: The clue describes the structure, so the answer is nest rather than the name of a bird. Not all birds build the same kind of nest.
answerNotes.BEE: The honey-making detail distinguishes this answer from other striped insects. Bees also carry pollen as they visit flowers.
answerNotes.SNAIL: The coiled shell helps distinguish a snail from a slug. Both can turn up among garden plants.
answerNotes.WEB: A web is the structure, while a spider is its maker. Pairing these ideas can help you follow whether a clue asks for an animal or an object.

title: Starting from Seeds
cardDescription: The small steps from a seed packet to a young plant.
description: Follow a seed's beginning, from choosing a pot and adding water to spotting the first shoot, in this easy growing-themed puzzle.
focus: The answers follow the early stages of growing a plant: containers, moisture, planting depth, and new growth. The clues explain their context directly. This is a vocabulary puzzle, not a planting calendar; the right conditions depend on the seed being grown.
solvingTip: Think about what happens above and below the soil. A root grows downward, while a shoot develops upward. Action clues such as 'Plant seeds in soil' call for a verb rather than the name of a tool.
words: Small plant structure sown to grow a new plant
Earth in which a young plant can take root
Plant container commonly made of clay or plastic
Flat container that can hold several small seed pots
Liquid used to moisten a seed's growing medium
What a sunny window or a grow lamp provides
Plant part that takes up water from below the soil
Young upward-growing part of a plant
Begin to grow, as a seed does
Marker that identifies what was planted
Decayed organic material often added to garden soil

Let excess water flow out of a container
Gentle heat that many seeds need to begin growing

Remove extra seedlings so the remaining ones have room

answerNotes.ROOT: A root takes up water and anchors the plant. A shoot is the young upward-growing part, so the direction described in a clue helps you choose between them.
answerNotes.SOW: Sow means to plant seeds. It sounds like 'so,' but its spelling is tied to the gardening action described in the clue.
answerNotes.DAMP: Damp means slightly wet. It is different from soaked, which is why the clue emphasizes a little moisture rather than standing water.
answerNotes.THIN: In gardening, thin can be a verb meaning to remove some seedlings so others have more room. It does not refer to the shape of a seedling here.
answerNotes.DEPTH: Planting depth describes how far below the surface a seed is placed. Seed packets give different recommendations, so there is no single depth for every crop.
answerNotes.LABEL: A label identifies the contents of a pot or tray. It can record the plant name without relying on remembering where each seed was sown.
